theoretical

/thee-uh-RET-ih-kul/ — punch the RET: 'theo-RET-ical' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Theoretical is based on ideas and reasoning rather than practical experience.

Her knowledge of sailing was purely theoretical until she finally stepped onto a boat.

Example

The engineering students' design for a solar-powered car was purely theoretical: they calculated on paper exactly how fast it should go, but none of them had ever built one, and their numbers had never touched a real road.

Theoretical means based on ideas and reasoning rather than hands-on experience. 'Practical' knowledge comes from doing; theoretical knowledge lives in models, formulas, and untested plans.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hypothetical: Hypothetical describes something assumed or invented so an idea can be examined — a what-if case nobody claims is real. Theoretical is broader and more serious: knowledge built from ideas and careful reasoning that has not yet been tested against practical experience.

abstract: Abstract means existing in thought rather than in physical form — justice, freedom, and numbers are abstract. Theoretical says how knowledge was built: from ideas and reasoning instead of hands-on practice. A theoretical design can describe a very concrete machine.

speculative: Speculative means resting on guesswork because solid evidence is missing — speculative rumors, speculative investments. Theoretical work is not guessing: it reasons carefully from established ideas, but it has not yet been checked against practical experience.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

practical: based on real use and experience

concrete: real, specific, and tangible

Where it sits · how far from reality it sits

unproven → theoretical → imaginary

unproven vs. theoretical: Unproven is weaker than theoretical — an unproven idea merely lacks final confirmation, while a theoretical one may never have left the world of ideas at all.

imaginary vs. theoretical: Imaginary is stronger than theoretical — a theoretical idea is a serious untested model, but an imaginary one exists only in fantasy with no basis in reasoning.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — theoret-: to look at, contemplate (Greek theoria, 'a viewing'; theoret- is the stem of theoretikos, 'given to contemplation')

Suffix — -ical: relating to (Greek/Latin)

Put it together: Greek theoria meant 'a viewing or contemplation': theoret- (the Greek stem, as in theoretikos) + -ical ('relating to'). Theoretical knowledge is what you gain by looking at and thinking about something, rather than by doing it.

Use the root in a new word: theorem: She copied the theorem neatly into her math notebook.
